world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: While there are a few nonpredictable and thus contrastive long vowels, most surface vowel length is allophonic, due to synchronic rules of lengthening under the accent ... There is limited but solid evidence for a synchronic rule in Palaic whereby the word accent shifts one syllable to the right with the addition of an enclitic (cf. the similar rule in Latin): underlying /ħáran-/ “eagle” appears as regular [ħá:ranas] in the genitive singular ḫāranaš, but compare nominative singular [ħará:s] in the phrase ḫarāš=kuwar. ... There are actually two such synchronic lengthening rules, one applying to all accented vowels in open syllables, the other to /a/ and /e/ in accented closed syllables (see Melchert 1994:204f. for further discussion).
new_statements.citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 2004. Palaic. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, 585-590. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (repr. 2008 in Woodard ed., The Ancient Languages of Asia Minor, 40-45).
new_statements.locator: p. 587, §3.2 'Vowels' (last sentences) and §3.3 'Synchronic variation' (first paragraph); PDF page 48
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: is a 64-page scan (no text layer) of the Anatolian chapters of Woodard (ed.) 2004; PDF p. 48 = printed p. 587 'PALAIC', H. Craig Melchert. I rendered the page image and read it directly (not only the scanned txt). The three quoted stretches are there verbatim: sec. 3.2 'While there are a few nonpredictable and thus contrastive long vowels, most surface vowel length is allophonic, due to synchronic rules of lengthening under the accent: for examples see the next paragraph.'; sec. 3.3 'There is limited but solid evidence for a synchronic rule in Palaic whereby the word accent shifts one syllable to the right with the addition of an enclitic (cf. the similar rule in Latin): underly…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Palaic has a word accent whose position is not fixed by a phonological rule: it is lexically/morphologically given (inherited IE mobile accent, e.g. root-accented /ħáran-/ 'eagle', ending-accented pres. 3pl. -ānti), and is recoverable only from plene spellings because accented vowels are lengthened (all accented vowels in open syllables; /a/, /e/ also in closed syllables). The one synchronic positional rule stated is that adding an enclitic shifts the accent one syllable to the right. Note the competing view of Kassian & Shatskov 2013:100, who state that nothing is known about Palaic stress and read plene spellings as length only.
new_statements.exceptions: A few long vowels are non-predictable (contrastive) rather than accent-conditioned; plene writing is not obligatory, so absence of plene spelling is not evidence of lack of accent (Melchert 1984 fn. 17).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including enclitics (accent shifts rightward when an enclitic is attached: ḫarāš=kuwar). All evidence is orthographic (cuneiform plene spellings) from a very small corpus; Melchert 1993 §9 characterises Anatolian accent as having 'an element of stress as well as pitch'.
new_statements.identity_note: Palaic as attested in Hittite cuneiform tablets (17th-13th c. BC); all evidence for accent is indirect, inferred from plene (scriptio plena) vowel spellings interpreted as accent-conditioned length. No dialect issue; glottocode pala1331.

sources.note: p. 587 §3.2-3.3: most surface vowel length is allophonic, from synchronic lengthening under the accent; the word accent shifts one syllable rightward when an enclitic is added (/ħáran-/ 'eagle': gen. [ħá:ranas] ḫāranaš vs. nom. [ħará:s] in ḫarāš=kuwar); two lengthening rules (accented open syllables; /a/,/e/ in accented closed syllables); refers to Melchert 1994:204f. No rule fixing the position of the accent is given — accent position is lexical/inherited.

sources.citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 1993. Historical Phonology of Anatolian. Journal of Indo-European Studies 21(3-4): 237-257.
sources.note: §5.4 (p. 246): Palaic, like Hittite and Luvian, lengthens all short vowels in accented open syllables and lengthens /a/ (and /e/) in accented closed syllables (*wérti > wēerti); §9 'Accent' (p. 254): 'I have made no attempt to describe the accent systematically in the various languages... the accent in Anatolian contains an element of stress as well as pitch... the position of the accent is mostly maintained into the attested languages.'
